evals.prompt: Define visual design foundations in 2-3 sentences. What does it cover and at what level?
expected_elements: Shaping the visual craft of an interface — palette, type scale, spacing rhythm, density, elevation, hierarchy, contrast intent, motion feel, brand fit
It is foundation level, not deep color/typography/motion/token engineering
Visual design makes structure legible — it is not decoration applied after structure
It hands off deeper concerns to the skills that own those contracts

evals.prompt: Why choose palette roles and type roles before picking raw colors and sizes?
expected_elements: Roles encode purpose (surface, text, accent, success/warning/danger/info, disabled; title/heading/label/body/metadata/numeric) before any raw value
Choosing by role keeps decisions consistent and changeable rather than ad hoc per screen
Raw colors/sizes picked first produce inconsistency and invisible hierarchy
Roles make priority and grouping derivable rather than hand-tuned

evals.prompt: Why set spacing and density rules against repeated real use rather than a single screenshot, and what's the trade-off with elevation/borders?
expected_elements: One screenshot hides how density holds up across real, repeated, data-varying use
Density must match the surface's repeated-use context (e.g. dense operational tool vs editorial page)
Elevation, border, and background should be used only to clarify grouping or affordance
Used decoratively, elevation/borders add noise rather than clarifying structure

evals.prompt: A dashboard 'feels flat and hard to scan.' Walk through how to improve the visual hierarchy without changing the task structure.
expected_elements: Name the surface type and intended tone/scanning demand first
Make primary content faster to find via type roles, weight, and spacing — not more color
Use elevation/borders only to clarify grouping or affordance
Preserve the task structure (this is craft, not layout/structure work)

evals.prompt: You are starting visual direction for an internal admin tool. Walk through the method steps in order.
expected_elements: Name the surface type (operational tool) and state tone + scanning demand
Choose palette roles before raw colors; define type roles (title, heading, label, body, metadata, numeric)
Set spacing/density for repeated use; use elevation/border/background only to clarify grouping or affordance
Check decisions against semiotics and a11y before treating them as done

evals.prompt: Someone asks visual-design-foundations to define the semantic design tokens and component variant APIs, and separately to verify WCAG contrast. Are these in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Token definitions, component APIs, theming contracts, and governance are out of scope — that is design-system-architecture
WCAG contrast/focus/labels/keyboard/AT verification is out of scope — that is a11y
visual-design-foundations owns the craft choices (palette/type/rhythm/density/polish) at foundation level, not those contracts
Correctly redirects each to its owning skill rather than absorbing it

evals.prompt: A stakeholder says 'visual design is the decoration you add at the end to make it look nice.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: Visual design is not decoration after structure — it is how structure becomes legible
It makes priority, grouping, affordance, and tone visible without the user parsing every label
Weak craft produces a surface that is harder to use, not merely plainer
It is also foundation-level: deeper color math/font engineering/token governance route to their owning skills

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a visual design pass is sound?
expected_elements: Visual hierarchy makes primary content faster to find; palette roles named by purpose not raw color
Type roles consistent and not oversized inside compact UI; spacing/density fit the repeated-use context
Elevation and borders clarify grouping rather than add noise; motion (if used) clarifies state/continuity and can be reduced
A11y contrast and non-color-only checks are deferred to a11y rather than asserted here
